item.title: A rare bird on stony rivers shows why Himalayan water needs its sediment
item.description: The Himalayan rivers are home to several species that depend on rivers and their ecosystems, including fish, aquatic invertebrates like stonefly larvae and mayfly nymphs, and flora such as Himalayan alder and sea buckthorn along the banks and on the floodplains. When a river changes, all these environs, and their species, change as well

item.title: Hostile architecture: the design choices keeping wildlife out of urban India
item.description: For animals and birds in India’s urban areas, hostile architecture takes many forms. ‘From spikes on ledges and nets over balconies to broken glass or spikes on compound walls that prevent animals from entering or perching,’ Shilpa Shirish, who specialises in culturally sensitive design at the Indian Institute of Human Settlements, Bengaluru, said

item.title: Meet the little stint: The tiny Siberian traveller visiting India’s wetlands
item.description: The Little Stint travels thousands of kilometres between its Arctic breeding grounds and Indian wetlands. But as shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands

item.title: Wildlife, forests, and culture in Gudalur: Sculptures, stories, and interactive workshops
item.description: Into the Forest, an ongoing exhibition in Gudalur explores the relationship between forests, wildlife and people through sculptures, stories, workshops for children and creative artefacts made using invasive plant species

item.title: COP31 and the unmet promises of climate action
item.description: COP31 has once again laid out the gap between what countries promise and what they are actually prepared to do. With the window to keep warming below 1.5 degrees rapidly closing, the coming year should be spent on fixing what is broken
